metadata.note: Passenger rail at Fort Myers and in Southwest Florida generally, which the map was missing entirely. Two railroads reached Fort Myers. The Atlantic Coast Line got there first, extending the ex-Plant System Lakeland–Punta Gorda line across the Caloosahatchee at Beautiful Island; regular passenger service began 10 May 1904 and Fort Myers was the southernmost point on the whole ACL until the 1920s. The land boom then produced a duplicate: the Seaboard Air Line, through its Seaboard–All Florida Railway and Naples, Seaboard and Gulf Railway subsidiaries, built 68 miles from Hull near Fort Ogden through Fort Myers to Naples, opening it on 7 January 1927 with a special section of the Orange Blossom Special. The ACL meanwhile pushed its own Fort Myers Southern Branch south to Bonita Springs (1925), Naples (1926) and Collier City on Marco Island (1927). The boom collapsed almost immediately: the Seaboard went bankrupt in 1930, cut back to a three-day-a-week mixed train in 1931 and quit carrying passengers in 1933, abandoning Naples–Punta Rassa Junction in 1942 and the rest by 1952. The ACL bought the Seaboard's Naples depot and the last seven miles of its right of way in 1942 and in 1944 rerouted its own Naples trains down it into downtown, abandoning its line south of Vanderbilt. A daily Lakeland–Naples train survived the 1967 ACL/SAL merger into the Seaboard Coast Line and ran until Amtrak began on 1 May 1971 without Southwest Florida. Passenger trains returned in 1991 when Seminole Gulf Railway, which has operated Arcadia–North Naples since 1987, began excursions, and its Murder Mystery Dinner Train has run out of Fort Myers since 1993 and still does.

metadata.not_yet_sourced: Every headway_min in this file is an estimate except where a segment note says otherwise; only the 1967 ACL timetable gives real timings. The exact year general Seminole Gulf excursions ended (given only as 'the late 1990s'; 1999 assumed) and the extent of the 1991-93 North Naples excursion, which is not drawn. metadata.freight_only_note: Deliberately excluded under Rule 1: the Seaboard's Punta Rassa Subdivision (Punta Rassa Junction – Biggar – San Carlos – Truckland, VN 934.3–942.7), which the source describes as serving agricultural land and gladiolus fields with no passenger service documented; the seven-mile 1940s spur from the LaBelle branch to Buckingham Army Air Field; and Seminole Gulf Railway's ordinary freight operation, which is drawn here only for the years and over the miles its passenger excursions and dinner trains actually run.

segments.note: Regular passenger service to Fort Myers began 10 May 1904 over new trestles across the Caloosahatchee at Beautiful Island, reached via Tice. The first Fort Myers depot stood at Main and Monroe streets; the ACL replaced it in 1924 with the Spanish mission-style station at Jackson and Peck. Fort Myers was the southernmost point on the entire Atlantic Coast Line until the 1920s land boom. Headway is an estimate.

properties.geometry_quality: The pre-1944 alignment, east of Naples. Traced from OSM ways tagged old_railway_operator=ACL and from the abandoned way named 'Fort Myers Southern Railroad'; 36.9 mi traced against about 36 mi documented. Two straight-line connectors totalling 2.86 mi (mostly a 2.4 km gap in the mapped abandoned grade north of the airport). segments.note: Passenger service to Naples began 27 December 1926, eleven days before the Seaboard's rival line opened. The Atlantic Coast Line had been pushed onto the east side of town because the Seaboard quietly secured the better right of way into downtown; the original ACL depot stood at what is now Airport Road and Radio Road, and Naples trains had to be turned on the wye at Bonita Springs and backed down, there being no wye at Naples. Headway is an estimate.

segments.note: After the Seaboard abandoned its parallel line in 1942 the ACL bought its Naples depot on Fifth Avenue South and the southernmost seven miles of its right of way up to Vanderbilt. In 1944 the ACL connected the Fort Myers Southern Branch to that right of way near Vanderbilt Beach and rebuilt track down it into downtown Naples, abandoning its own line south of Vanderbilt. A daily local ran through from Lakeland; a mixed train ran Fort Myers–Naples six days a week in the 1940s.

properties.line: Atlantic Coast Line: Naples – Marco Island
properties.speed_source: estimated: a mixed train over a lightly built branch; no timetable consulted
properties.geometry_quality: Traced from the two OSM abandoned ways tagged old_railway_operator=ACL that carry this grade south-east of Naples; no connectors. Traced 12.9 mi, against roughly 15 mi implied by the mileposts (AX 1001.2 Naples – AX 1016.5 Collier City) — but those are post-1944 mileposts measured from the Fifth Avenue depot, whereas this feature starts at the original depot near the airport, so the two figures are not directly comparable. segments.note: The Fort Myers Southern Branch was pushed on to Collier City at the north end of Marco Island in mid-1927, where a wye was built. Service was a mixed train out of Fort Myers and Naples; the Doxsee clam factory was the branch's reason for existing and its main freight customer. Regularly scheduled trains to Marco Island had ceased by 1940, and the factory moved to Naples in 1943. Headway is an estimate.

properties.line: Seaboard Air Line: Fort Myers Subdivision
properties.speed_source: estimated: a land-boom main line built for the Orange Blossom Special; no Seaboard timetable consulted
properties.geometry_quality: Composite, 69.2 mi traced against 68.3 mi documented (VC 893.4 Hull – VC 961.7 Naples). Hull–Fort Myers–Alico Road (32.5 mi, matching the documented 32.2 mi to Fort Myers) is real, from OSM ways tagged old_railway_operator=SAL, with 1.2 km of straight-line connector. South of that the grade is not mapped as railway at all, so: 6.2 mi of pure straight line (Alico Road – Mullock Creek – north of Estero); 11.0 mi on the centreline of the FPL transmission line that the sources say occupies the grade from Mullock Creek to Vanderbilt Beach (this correctly puts the Bonita Springs depot on the south side of Bonita Beach Road); a further 2.0 mi of straight line across a break in that power line north of Bonita Springs; and 8.7 mi on Goodlette-Frank Road, which occupies the grade from Immokalee Road into downtown Naples — against 8.0 mi documented for Vanderbilt – Naples. In short, roughly half this feature is a labelled approximation, not traced rail. Straight-line repair 2026-08-29: 1 ruled segment totalling 20 mi replaced with OpenStreetMap-traced rail geometry (see geometry_repairs for the OSM lines each one followed).

segments.note: The line opened for passengers on 7 January 1927, when Seaboard president S. Davies Warfield rode a special section of the Orange Blossom Special down it with Governor John W. Martin and thousands turned out at the stations — the same train inaugurated the Miami extension the next day. The Orange Blossom Special and the West Coast Limited then gave daily service down the west coast. Headway is an estimate of that combined service.

segments.note: Seminole Gulf began running passenger excursions in 1991 after losing a large freight customer, the first on 5 January 1991 from a platform in North Naples near Railhead Park. The 1991-93 North Naples operation is not drawn here because its extent is not sourced, and the end year and the weekly headway are both estimates.
